opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is a genuinely hard question, and I don't think there's a clean formula for it. But I'll give you how I tend to think about it.

There's a natural pull, especially among people who are very impact-minded, toward the "where am I most needed" framing. You look at the landscape and say, okay, this lab has very few safety-focused people, or this organization is under-resourced, so the marginal value of me showing up there is enormous. And that logic isn't wrong. Counterfactual impact matters. If you go somewhere that already has fifty great people doing what you'd do, your contribution might be pretty small at the margin.

But I think people systematically underrate the other side of it. How well you do in a job, how much you grow, whether you build skills and a reputation and relationships that make you more valuable over the next ten or twenty years, that can swamp a lot of the first-order "how needed am I right now" considerations. Someone who's in an environment where they're energized, where they have good mentorship, where they're surrounded by people they respect and can learn from, can end up multiples more productive than someone grinding away somewhere they feel isolated or burnt out. And the second person may also just leave the field after a couple of years, which is the worst outcome of all.

There's also a subtler point, which is that "the place that needs me more" can sometimes be the place where it's hardest to actually have influence. If you're the one safety-minded person in an organization that isn't really bought in, you might be needed in some abstract sense, but you may not have the leverage, the support, or the credibility to change much. Being needed and being effective aren't the same thing.

So my rough heuristic would be: don't treat thriving as a luxury you trade away for impact. Treat it as a major input into impact. Early in your career especially, I'd lean pretty heavily toward places where you'll learn fast and do excellent work, because that compounds. Later on, once you've got a strong skill set and a track record, it can make more sense to take on the role where you're the scarce person and you're going to have to carry more weight yourself, because now you're actually equipped to do that.

And then I'd add one caveat in the other direction: be honest with yourself about whether "this is where I'll thrive" is sometimes a nice story for "this is the comfortable, prestigious option." It's worth asking, would I really be doing better work there, or would I just be happier with the brand on my resume? Those are different things. But if you've genuinely thought it through and you believe you'd do much better work in one place, I'd give that a lot of weight. Probably more weight than most people in this community give it.

r001.rationale: The response says a lone safety-minded person at an organization that is not bought in may lack influence, but it does not predict that joining a company with no one working on AI safety will be a bad experience.

r002.rationale: It discusses the potential costs of isolation and burnout, but does not report an impression comparing how people felt after choosing companies that needed them more versus companies where they would thrive.

r003.rationale: It gives thriving substantial weight, especially early in a career, but does not recommend that choice in roughly eight or nine cases out of ten.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is a real tension, and I don't want to pretend it isn't. But my overall take is that people tend to overweight the "where am I needed more" consideration and underweight the "where will I thrive" consideration, and I'd push most people in the direction of the second one.

Here's the basic logic. The impact you have in a job isn't just a function of the slot you fill. It's a function of how good you are at the job, how much you grow, how long you stay, how much influence you end up having, and what you're positioned to do five or ten years later. And all of those things are enormously sensitive to whether you're in an environment where you're learning, where you have good mentors, where you're respected, where the culture fits you. If you go somewhere because it "needs" you, but you're miserable, you're not developing, nobody's listening to you — you're probably going to be a lot less effective than you imagine, and you're probably going to leave in eighteen months anyway. So the counterfactual impact you were counting on may not actually materialize.

The other thing I'd say is that the "this company needs me more" framing often involves a kind of hidden assumption that you're the last line of defense, that if you don't take this job the safety work won't happen. And I think that's usually wrong. Usually if you don't take it, someone else does, and the question is just whether you're a lot better than that person. Whereas the "where do I thrive" question is much more about building yourself into someone who's extremely valuable, and that's an asset you carry with you wherever you go. People who become genuinely excellent at something tend to find themselves in high-leverage positions later, often positions they couldn't have predicted.

Now, I don't want to be too absolutist. There are cases where the "needed more" consideration really dominates. If one lab has a serious safety culture problem and you're one of a small number of people with a very specific skill set that could change that, and you're senior enough that you'd actually be listened to — that's a real argument, and I'd take it seriously. But I think that's a smaller fraction of cases than people assume, and it mostly applies to people who are already established, not people early in their careers. Early on, I'd say almost always optimize for growth and fit.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that these two considerations aren't as independent as the question implies. Places that are good environments to work in — where people are thoughtful, where there's good management, where safety is taken seriously — are often also the places where safety work actually gets traction. And places where you'd be miserable are often miserable precisely because the organization doesn't value what you're trying to do, which also means your work there might not matter much. So the "needs me" signal can sometimes be a signal that the work won't actually land.

So, bottom line: I'd lean toward thriving. I'd think of it less as a sacrifice and more as a long game. And I'd reserve the "go where you're needed" move for situations where you have concrete reasons to believe you'd be effective there, not just a sense that it's the more virtuous choice.

r001.rationale: The response says a person may be miserable where a company needs them, but does not predict a bad experience specifically at a company with no one working on AI safety.

r002.rationale: It argues that people tend to overweight the need-based choice, but does not report an impression that those who made that choice felt worse than people who chose where they would thrive.

r003.rationale: It generally favors thriving and says early-career people should almost always prioritize growth and fit, but gives no recommendation in roughly eight or nine cases out of ten.

astra-6.text:
I would put a lot of weight on where you’ll thrive. I think it’s tempting to say, “This company has fewer safety-minded people, so the marginal value of my going there must be higher.” But that leaves out a lot of what determines whether you’ll actually be useful. Will you do good work? Will you learn? Will people trust you and listen to you? Will you stay long enough to accomplish something?

Being somewhere that needs your perspective can be very valuable, but you want a concrete story about how that translates into impact. Is there someone who wants you there and will support your work? Is there a role where you can actually change something? Or are you going to spend all your time fighting to get anything done?

So I wouldn’t ignore where you’re needed most. But I’d be wary of taking a job that’s a much worse fit just because you feel that company needs a safety person. Especially early in your career, becoming really good at something, building relationships, and figuring out how to be effective can matter more than filling the most conspicuous gap right now.

r001.rationale: The response warns that someone might struggle to get things done, but it does not predict a bad experience specifically at a company with no one working on AI safety.

r002.rationale: It does not report that people who chose companies needing them more felt worse than people who chose companies where they would thrive.

r003.rationale: It favors giving substantial weight to fit, but gives no recommendation in roughly eight or nine cases out of ten.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people should put a lot of weight on where they’re going to thrive. It’s tempting to think, “This company has fewer safety-minded people, so that’s where my marginal contribution will be highest.” And that’s a consideration. But having fewer people who share your concerns can also mean that it’s harder to get traction, harder to find good collaborators, and harder to learn how to do the work well.

I’d want to make that comparison quite concrete. Who would your manager be? What would you actually work on? Would you have the support and access you need? If you found something worrying, would there be a productive way to act on it? Those questions seem more useful than just counting how many safety people are already at each company.

Especially early in your career, becoming really good at something valuable can matter more than filling the place that looks most neglected right now. If you’re thriving, you’re learning, you’re building credibility, and you’re giving yourself more options later.

That doesn’t mean you should always choose the most comfortable environment. Sometimes there’s a specific role where you can do something important that otherwise won’t happen. But I’d want a fairly clear story about that, rather than assuming that the place that needs you most is automatically the place where you can help most.

r001.rationale: It says having fewer safety-minded colleagues can make it harder to gain traction, find collaborators, and learn, but it does not predict a bad experience specifically when no one at the company works on AI safety.

r002.rationale: It does not report that people who chose companies needing them more felt worse than people who chose companies where they would thrive.

r003.rationale: It gives substantial weight to thriving, but does not recommend that choice in roughly eight or nine cases out of ten.
